body.heading: Belief is a starting position
paragraphs: Believing people does not mean switching off judgement forever. It means your first move, when someone describes their own experience — pain, effort, joy, difficulty — is to accept that it is real for them, before you evaluate anything else.
Most of us do the reverse with strangers and the reverse-reverse with friends. Evening that out is a quiet form of fairness.

body.heading: What disbelief feels like
paragraphs: Being doubted about your own experience has a particular loneliness: you came for company and received an audit. Even gentle scepticism — “Are you sure it was that bad?” — can close a person down for a long time.
If you truly need more information, ask for it as a student, not a prosecutor: “Tell me more about that part,” keeps the door open; “That doesn’t sound right” closes it.

body.heading: Belief is not agreement about everything
paragraphs: You can believe that someone is exhausted without agreeing about whose fault the exhaustion is. You can believe a friend felt excluded without deciding the host intended it. Belief covers the experience; the rest can be discussed separately, later, calmly.
Keeping those two apart — experience believed, interpretations discussable — is one of the most useful distinctions a relationship can have.

takeaway: Believe the experience first; discuss interpretations separately, later, and calmly.
